title: Magnetic Circuits
description: Solve cores and air gaps like resistor circuits with mmf, flux and reluctance.

study.title: Magnetomotive force
study.body: A coil of $N$ turns carrying current $i$ drives flux around a core the way a battery drives current around a circuit. Its 'push' is the **magnetomotive force** (mmf) $\mathcal{F} = Ni$, measured in ampere-turns (A·t). The direction of the flux it drives follows the right-hand rule (fingers along the current in the turns, thumb along the flux).

study.title: Reluctance
study.body: A section of core with mean path length $\ell$, cross-section $A$ and permeability $\mu = \mu_r\mu_0$ opposes flux with a **reluctance** (A·t/Wb). Long, thin, low-permeability paths have high reluctance. Use SI units: lengths in m, areas in m² (1 cm² = $10^{-4}$ m²).

study.title: Ohm's law for magnetic circuits
study.body:
Flux, mmf and reluctance obey $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{R}\phi$, just like $V = RI$. Then $B = \phi/A$ in each section and $H = B/\mu$. So a magnetic circuit is drawn as a resistor circuit: the coil becomes a source $\mathcal{F} = Ni$, each core section a resistor $\mathcal{R}$, and the flux plays the role of current.
- mmf acts like voltage, flux like current, reluctance like resistance and permeability like conductivity.

study.title: Series and parallel paths
study.body: Reluctances combine exactly like resistors: in series they add, in parallel they combine as $\mathcal{R}_1\parallel\mathcal{R}_2$. The KVL analogue: around any closed path the mmf drops $H\ell$ (i.e. $\mathcal{R}\phi$) add up to the enclosed ampere-turns. The KCL analogue: the fluxes entering a junction of core legs sum to zero. In a three-legged core with the coil on the centre leg, the two outer legs are in parallel.

study.title: Air gaps
study.body: An air gap has $\mu_r = 1$, so a gap of only 1 mm has the same reluctance as 3 m of iron with $\mu_r = 3000$. A gap therefore usually **dominates** the total reluctance and sets the flux. Gaps are added on purpose to make the inductance predictable and to avoid saturation. We neglect **fringing** (the flux spreading out at the gap), so the gap has the same area as the core. The graph is the core of the worked example (500 A·t, $\ell_c$ = 40 cm, $A$ = 10 cm²). Drag $\mu_r$: without a gap it sets the flux; with 1 mm of gap a 5× change of $\mu_r$ moves the flux by only about 30 %. (Linear model: below about 0.2 mm of gap the readout $B$ exceeds 2 T, but real iron saturates around 1.5–2 T, so the flux there would be lower.)

study.title: Worked example: core with a gap
study.body:
A core with $\ell_c$ = 40 cm, $A$ = 10 cm², $\mu_r$ = 3000 has a 1 mm gap and a 500-turn coil carrying 1 A.
- $\mathcal{R}_c$ = 0.4 / (3000 · 4π×$10^{-7}$ · $10^{-3}$) = 1.06×$10^{5}$ A·t/Wb
- $\mathcal{R}_g$ = $10^{-3}$ / (4π×$10^{-7}$ · $10^{-3}$) = 7.96×$10^{5}$ A·t/Wb
- $\phi$ = 500 / 9.02×$10^{5}$ = 554 µWb, $B$ = 0.554 T
The gap takes 88 % of the mmf. **Pitfalls:** forgetting cm-to-m conversions, and using the inside length of the core instead of the mean path length.

steps.title: The coil as a source
steps.body: A coil of $N$ turns carrying $i$ pushes flux around its core. This push is the **magnetomotive force** (mmf), measured in ampere-turns (A·t). Ten turns with 1 A push as hard as one turn with 10 A.

steps.prompt: A {{N}}-turn coil carries {{i}} A. Find the magnetomotive force it applies to the core.

steps.title: Reluctance
steps.body: Each part of the flux path opposes the flux with a **reluctance**, which grows with the path length $\ell$ and shrinks with the cross-section $A$ and the permeability $\mu = \mu_r\mu_0$. It is the magnetic version of $R = \ell/(\sigma A)$.

steps.prompt: An iron core has a mean path length of {{l*100}} cm, a cross-section of {{Acm}} cm² and $\mu_r$ = {{mur}}. Find its reluctance.
Match each magnetic quantity with its electric-circuit analogue
steps.explanation: $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{R}\phi$ mirrors $V = RI$: mmf drives flux through reluctance as voltage drives current through resistance. $\mathcal{R} = \ell/(\mu A)$ mirrors $R = \ell/(\sigma A)$, so permeability plays the part of conductivity.

steps.title: Magnetic Ohm's law
steps.body: The flux follows from the mmf and the total reluctance, exactly like current in a resistor circuit. The flux density in a section of area $A$ is then $B = \phi/A$. A core with an air gap is two reluctances in series:

steps.title: Try it: the gap takes over
steps.body: A 500 A·t coil on an iron core ($\ell_c$ = 40 cm, $A$ = 10 cm²) with an air gap. Drag the gap length: the flux falls quickly because $\mathcal{R}_g$ grows linearly with $\ell_g$. Then drag the core's $\mu_r$: with a gap of 1 mm the flux changes far less than without a gap, because the gap takes most of the mmf (readout). (Linear model: below about 0.2 mm of gap $B$ exceeds 2 T, where real iron would already saturate.)

steps.prompt: A {{N}}-turn coil carrying {{i}} A is wound on a magnetic circuit with a total reluctance of {{R|A·t/Wb}}. Find the flux.
A core is replaced by one of the same material and length but with **twice** the cross-sectional area. What happens to its reluctance?
steps.explanation: $\mathcal{R} = \ell/(\mu A)$ is inversely proportional to $A$, so doubling the area halves the reluctance (like a wire with twice the cross-section has half the resistance). For the same mmf the flux doubles, while $B = \phi/A$ stays the same.

steps.prompt: An air gap of 1 mm can have a larger reluctance than 30 cm of iron with $\mu_r$ = 3000 and the same cross-section.
steps.explanation: True. With equal areas, compare $\ell/\mu_r$: the gap gives 1 mm / 1 = 1 mm, the iron 300 mm / 3000 = 0.1 mm. The tiny gap has **ten times** the reluctance of the iron path.

steps.prompt: A toroidal core has a mean radius of {{r*100}} cm, a cross-section of {{Acm}} cm² and $\mu_r$ = {{mur}}. It carries {{N}} turns with {{i}} A. Find the flux in the core.
steps.explanation:
Mean path length $\ell = 2\pi r$ = {{l}} m, $A$ = {{Acm*1e-4}} m².
$\mathcal{R} = \frac{\ell}{\mu_r\mu_0A}$ = {{R||4}} A·t/Wb.
$\phi = Ni/\mathcal{R}$ = {{N*i}} / {{R||4}} = {{phi|Wb}} (so $B$ = {{B|T}}).

steps.prompt: Find the reluctance of an air gap {{g*1000}} mm long with a cross-section of {{Acm}} cm² (neglect fringing).
A core ($\ell_c$ = {{lc*100}} cm, $A$ = {{Acm}} cm², $\mu_r$ = {{mur}}) has an air gap of {{g*1000}} mm with the same area (neglect fringing). A {{N}}-turn coil carries {{i}} A.

ask.prompt: Find the flux in the core.
Find the flux density in the air gap.
ask.explanation: $\mathcal{R}_c$ = {{Rc||4}}, $\mathcal{R}_g$ = {{Rg||4}} A·t/Wb, so $\phi$ = {{N*i}} / {{Rc+Rg||4}} = {{phi|Wb}}. Without fringing the gap has the core area: $B = \phi/A$ = {{phi|Wb}} / {{A}} m² = {{B|T}}. (Shortcut: $B = \mu_0Ni/(\ell_g + \ell_c/\mu_r)$.)

ask.prompt: Find the total reluctance of the magnetic circuit.

steps.prompt: A core with mean length {{lc*100}} cm and $\mu_r$ = {{mur}} has a {{g*1000}} mm air gap of the same cross-section. What current in a {{N}}-turn coil gives a flux density of {{Bg}} T in the gap? (Neglect fringing.)
steps.explanation:
The same flux and area pass through core and gap, so $B$ is {{Bg}} T in both. Ampère's law: $Ni = H_c\ell_c + H_g\ell_g = \frac{B}{\mu_0}\left(\frac{\ell_c}{\mu_r} + \ell_g\right)$.
$Ni$ = {{Bg/(4*pi*1e-7)}} × ({{lc/mur}} + {{g}}) = {{Ni}} A·t, so $i$ = {{Ni}} / {{N}} = {{Ni/N|A}}. The area is not needed.

steps.prompt: A core with $\ell_c$ = 20 cm, $\mu_r$ = 2000 and $A$ = 4 cm² carries {{N}} turns. The peak current is {{I}} A. Choose the air gap so that the flux density reaches exactly {{Bt}} T at the peak current: the line $B(i)$ must pass through the orange point. (Neglect fringing.)
steps.explanation: With the same $B$ in core and gap: $Ni = B\left(\frac{\ell_c}{\mu_r} + \ell_g\right)/\mu_0$. So $\ell_g = \frac{\mu_0 N i}{B} - \frac{\ell_c}{\mu_r}$ = {{4*pi*1e-7*N*I/Bt*1000}} mm − 0.1 mm = **{{gt*1000}} mm**. A bigger gap flattens the line, so the core reaches saturation only at a higher current; the price is a lower inductance, $L = N^2\mu_0A/(\ell_g + \ell_c/\mu_r)$ = {{N^2*4*pi*1e-7*4e-4/(gt+0.0001)|H}}.

steps.prompt: A core of mean length {{lc*100}} cm with $\mu_r$ = {{mur}} has an air gap of {{g*1000}} mm (same area, no fringing). What percentage of the coil's mmf is used across the **gap**?
steps.explanation: Series reluctances divide the mmf like a voltage divider: $\frac{\mathcal{R}_g}{\mathcal{R}_c+\mathcal{R}_g}$. With equal areas the factor $\mu_0A$ cancels, leaving $\frac{\ell_g}{\ell_g + \ell_c/\mu_r}$ = {{g}} / ({{g}} + {{lc/mur}}) = {{100*g/(g + lc/mur)|%}}.

steps.prompt: A coil with a fixed mmf drives flux through an iron core with an adjustable air gap $\ell_g$. Which graph shows the flux $\phi$ against $\ell_g$?
steps.explanation: $\phi = \frac{\mathcal{F}}{\mathcal{R}_c + \ell_g/(\mu_0A)}$. At $\ell_g = 0$ only the core reluctance limits the flux, so $\phi$ starts at a **finite** value $\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{R}_c$. As the gap grows, its reluctance grows linearly and the flux falls like $1/(a + b\ell_g)$: steeply at first, then slowly, never reaching zero. The $1/\ell_g$ curve that shoots up at $\ell_g = 0$ ignores the core reluctance.

steps.prompt: Two coils are wound on the same core (total reluctance {{R|A·t/Wb}}): {{N1}} turns carrying {{i1}} A and {{N2}} turns carrying {{i2}} A. The coils are connected so that their mmfs **oppose** each other. Find the magnitude of the core flux.
steps.explanation:
The mmfs are like two series voltage sources in opposition: net $\mathcal{F} = |N_1i_1 - N_2i_2|$ = |{{N1*i1}} − {{N2*i2}}| = {{abs(N1*i1-N2*i2)}} A·t.
$\phi = \mathcal{F}/\mathcal{R}$ = {{abs(N1*i1-N2*i2)}} / {{R}} = {{abs(N1*i1-N2*i2)/R|Wb}}. (Aiding, they would give {{(N1*i1+N2*i2)/R|Wb}}.)

steps.prompt: A magnetic circuit consists of an iron core with a gap whose reluctance is much larger than that of the iron. The gap length is **doubled**. What happens to the flux (same coil current)?
options: It hardly changes, because the iron sets the flux
It drops to about a quarter
steps.explanation: With $\mathcal{R}_g \gg \mathcal{R}_c$, $\phi \approx Ni/\mathcal{R}_g$, and $\mathcal{R}_g = \ell_g/(\mu_0A)$ doubles with the gap length. So the flux roughly halves. It ends up slightly **above** half of its old value, because the small core reluctance does not double.

steps.prompt: This is the analogue circuit of a core with two parallel legs ($\mathcal{R}_a$, $\mathcal{R}_b$). Tap every reluctance that carries the **full** flux produced by the coil.
steps.explanation: $\mathcal{R}_y$ and $\mathcal{R}_z$ are in series with the source $\mathcal{F}$, so the whole flux passes through them. At the junction the flux splits between the parallel legs $\mathcal{R}_a$ and $\mathcal{R}_b$ (KCL analogue), the smaller reluctance taking the larger share.

steps.prompt: The analogue circuit models a three-legged core with the coil on the centre leg ($\mathcal{R}_m$). The right leg contains an air gap. All reluctances are in A·t/Wb (k = $10^{3}$).

ask.prompt: Find the flux in the centre leg.
ask.explanation:
The outer legs are in parallel: $\mathcal{R}_1\parallel\mathcal{R}_2$ = {{par(R1,R2)||4}}. In series with the centre leg: $\mathcal{R}_t$ = {{Rt||4}} A·t/Wb.
$\phi_m = Ni/\mathcal{R}_t$ = {{N*i}} / {{Rt||4}} = {{pc|Wb}}.

ask.prompt: Find the flux in the right leg ($\mathcal{R}_2$).
ask.explanation:
$\mathcal{R}_t = \mathcal{R}_m + \mathcal{R}_1\parallel\mathcal{R}_2$ = {{Rt||4}} A·t/Wb, so $\phi_m$ = {{N*i}} / {{Rt||4}} = {{pc|Wb}}.
The flux divides like current: $\phi_2 = \phi_m\frac{\mathcal{R}_1}{\mathcal{R}_1+\mathcal{R}_2}$ = {{pc|Wb}} × {{R1/(R1+R2)}} = {{pc*R1/(R1+R2)|Wb}}.

ask.prompt: Find the flux in the left leg ($\mathcal{R}_1$).
ask.explanation:
$\mathcal{R}_t = \mathcal{R}_m + \mathcal{R}_1\parallel\mathcal{R}_2$ = {{Rt||4}} A·t/Wb, so $\phi_m$ = {{N*i}} / {{Rt||4}} = {{pc|Wb}}.
Flux divider: $\phi_1 = \phi_m\frac{\mathcal{R}_2}{\mathcal{R}_1+\mathcal{R}_2}$ = {{pc|Wb}} × {{R2/(R1+R2)}} = {{pc*R2/(R1+R2)|Wb}}. The leg without the gap carries more flux.

steps.prompt: A core ($\mu_r$ = {{mur}}) has two sections in series: {{l1*100}} cm long with {{A1cm}} cm² and {{l2*100}} cm long with only {{A2cm}} cm². A {{N}}-turn coil carries {{i}} A. Find the flux density in the **narrow** section.
steps.explanation:
$\mathcal{R}_1$ = {{l1}} / ({{mur}} $\mu_0$ × {{A1cm*1e-4}}) = {{R1||4}}, $\mathcal{R}_2$ = {{l2}} / ({{mur}} $\mu_0$ × {{A2cm*1e-4}}) = {{R2||4}} A·t/Wb.
$\phi = Ni/(\mathcal{R}_1+\mathcal{R}_2)$ = {{N*i}} / {{R1+R2||4}} = {{phi|Wb}}. The same flux squeezes through the narrow part: $B_2 = \phi/A_2$ = {{B2|T}} (the wide part has only {{phi/(A1cm*1e-4)|T}}). Narrow sections saturate first.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the measured core flux of a coil with a fixed mmf of {{F}} A·t as the air gap $\ell_g$ is varied. Use the value at $\ell_g = 0$ to find the reluctance of the iron core alone.
steps.explanation: With no gap only the core limits the flux: $\phi(0)$ = {{p0|Wb}}, so $\mathcal{R}_c = \mathcal{F}/\phi(0)$ = {{F}} / {{p0}} = {{Rc||3}} A·t/Wb. (Each extra mm of gap adds $\ell_g/(\mu_0A)$ = {{k*0.001||3}} A·t/Wb, which is why the curve drops so quickly.)

steps.prompt: Put the steps in order to find the coil current that gives a required flux density $B$ in a core with an air gap
items: Compute the reluctance of each section, $\ell/(\mu A)$
Divide by the number of turns: $i = \mathcal{F}/N$
steps.explanation: Work backwards from the flux: the flux and the reluctances give the required mmf, and the mmf divided by $N$ gives the current.

steps.prompt: In a three-legged core, the centre leg (reluctance {{Rm|A·t/Wb}}, area {{Acm}} cm²) carries the coil, and the outer legs have reluctances {{R1/1e5}}×$10^{5}$ and {{R2|A·t/Wb}}. What mmf gives a flux density of {{B}} T in the centre leg?
steps.explanation:
Required flux: $\phi = BA$ = {{B}} × {{Acm*1e-4}} = {{phi|Wb}}. The outer legs are in parallel: {{par(R1,R2)||4}}; total $\mathcal{R}_t$ = {{Rm}} + {{par(R1,R2)||4}} = {{Rt||4}} A·t/Wb.
$\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{R}_t\phi$ = {{Rt||4}} × {{phi}} = {{phi*Rt}} A·t (that is {{phi*Rt/N|A}} in {{N}} turns).
